CHAPTER 10 - HEAT TRANSFER AND SOLAR ENERGY

Introduction

Heat is energy in transit. Whenever two bodies (or two parts of the same body) are at different temperatures, energy flows from the hotter region to the colder region until the temperatures become equal. This spontaneous flow is called HEAT TRANSFER, and it always proceeds from higher to lower temperature. There are three distinct mechanisms by which heat is transferred: CONDUCTION, CONVECTION and RADIATION. This chapter studies all three, develops the laws that govern thermal radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann law, Newton's law of cooling, Wien's displacement law and Kirchhoff's law), and then applies these ideas to the greenhouse effect and to the practical harnessing of solar energy through solar cookers, solar cells and solar water heaters.

10.1 CONDUCTION

Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material WITHOUT any bulk movement of the material itself. The energy is handed on from molecule to molecule (and, in metals, largely by free electrons). Hold one end of a metal rod in a flame; after a while the other end becomes hot even though no part of the rod has moved. That is conduction.

Consider a slab of material of cross-sectional area A and thickness L, whose two faces are held at steady temperatures T1 and T2 (T1 greater than T2). In the steady state the quantity of heat Q that flows through the slab in time t is found experimentally to obey

   Q = K A (T1 - T2) t / L

The rate of flow of heat, called the HEAT CURRENT H, is therefore

   H = Q / t = K A (T1 - T2) / L

Here (T1 - T2)/L is the TEMPERATURE GRADIENT - the fall in temperature per unit length along the direction of flow. The constant K is the THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY of the material. Its SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin (W/m/K). A large K means the material conducts heat readily (metals: silver, copper, aluminium). A small K means the material is a poor conductor, i.e. a good insulator (wood, glass, air, wool, cork).

Thermal resistance. By analogy with electricity (where current I = potential difference / resistance), we may write the heat current as

   H = (T1 - T2) / R_th ,   with   R_th = L / (K A)

R_th is the THERMAL RESISTANCE of the slab, measured in K/W. A thick slab (large L), a small area, or a low conductivity all give a high thermal resistance and hence a small heat current. This is exactly why blankets, double walls and layers of trapped air keep us warm - they add thermal resistance.

Slabs in series and in parallel. When two slabs are joined one behind the other (series), the SAME heat current flows through both, and the total thermal resistance is the sum:

   R_series = R1 + R2 = L1/(K1 A) + L2/(K2 A)

When two slabs are placed side by side so that heat flows through both at once (parallel), they share the same temperature difference and their resistances combine like parallel resistors:

   1/R_parallel = 1/R1 + 1/R2

Worked example 1. A glass window pane is 4.0 mm thick and has area 1.5 m^2. The inside surface is at 20 C and the outside at 5 C. Take K(glass) = 0.80 W/m/K. Find the rate of heat loss.
Solution. H = K A (T1 - T2) / L = 0.80 x 1.5 x (20 - 5) / (4.0 x 10^-3) = 0.80 x 1.5 x 15 / 0.004 = 4500 W. A single thin pane loses heat very rapidly; a double-glazed unit with an air gap adds a large thermal resistance and cuts this loss dramatically.

10.2 CONVECTION

Convection is the transfer of heat by the ACTUAL BULK MOVEMENT of a heated fluid (a liquid or a gas). When a fluid is heated from below, the warm fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks to take its place. The resulting circulation, called a CONVECTION CURRENT, carries thermal energy from the hot region to the cold region.

There are two kinds of convection. In NATURAL (or free) convection the circulation is driven only by the density differences produced by heating - as in a pan of water warming on a stove, in the rising of warm air above a heater, in land and sea breezes, and in the large-scale circulation of the atmosphere and oceans. In FORCED convection an external agent - a fan, a pump or a blower - drives the fluid past the hot surface. The cooling system of a car (a water pump plus a radiator fan), a hair dryer, and the forced-air heating of a building are examples of forced convection; forced convection transfers heat much faster than natural convection.

Convection cannot occur in solids, because the particles of a solid are not free to move in bulk. It also cannot occur in a vacuum, since there is no medium to carry the energy. Everyday phenomena governed by convection include the formation of sea and land breezes, monsoon winds, trade winds, ventilation of rooms, and the working of a domestic hot-water system.

10.3 RADIATION AND THE BLACK BODY

Radiation is the transfer of heat by ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES, and it needs NO material medium at all. The energy of the Sun reaches the Earth across about 150 million kilometres of empty space entirely by radiation. Every body emits thermal radiation because of the thermal motion of its charged particles; the hotter the body, the more it radiates and the shorter the wavelengths involved. Thermal radiation is mostly infrared for bodies near room temperature, but becomes visible (red, then white) as the temperature rises, as in a heated iron bar or the filament of a lamp.

When radiation falls on a body, part of it is absorbed, part reflected and part transmitted. The fractions are the ABSORPTANCE a, the reflectance r and the transmittance, and a + r + (transmittance) = 1. A body that ABSORBS all the radiation falling on it (a = 1, reflecting and transmitting nothing) is called a PERFECT BLACK BODY. A perfect black body is also the best possible emitter of radiation at any given temperature. A small hole in a hollow cavity behaves very nearly as a black body: radiation entering the hole is reflected repeatedly inside and almost none escapes, so the hole absorbs practically everything.

The EMISSIVE POWER (or emittance) of a surface is the energy it radiates per unit area per unit time. For a black body this is written E_b; for a real surface it is E = e x E_b, where e (the EMISSIVITY, 0 < e <= 1) measures how good a radiator the surface is compared with a black body. A dull black surface has emissivity close to 1; a polished silvery surface has emissivity close to 0. Good absorbers are good emitters, and good reflectors are poor emitters - which is why a shiny surface both reflects incoming radiation and radiates little of its own.

10.4 STEFAN-BOLTZMANN LAW AND NEWTON'S LAW OF COOLING

Stefan-Boltzmann law. The total energy radiated per unit area per unit time by a black body is proportional to the FOURTH POWER of its absolute (kelvin) temperature:

   E = sigma T^4

where sigma is the STEFAN-BOLTZMANN CONSTANT, sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4. For a real body of emissivity e, E = e sigma T^4. Because of the fourth power, radiation rises extremely steeply with temperature: doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the radiated power by 2^4 = 16.

A body at temperature T sitting in surroundings at temperature T0 emits sigma T^4 and absorbs sigma T0^4 per unit area, so the NET rate of loss of heat per unit area is

   E_net = e sigma (T^4 - T0^4)

Worked example 2. A metal sphere of surface area 0.010 m^2 is at 500 K and behaves as a black body. How much energy does it radiate per second? Take sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8.
Solution. E = sigma T^4 = 5.67 x 10^-8 x (500)^4 = 5.67 x 10^-8 x 6.25 x 10^10 = 3543.75 W/m^2. Power = E x A = 3543.75 x 0.010 = 35.4 W (about 35 W).

Newton's law of cooling. For a body only a little hotter than its surroundings, the net radiation loss E_net = e sigma (T^4 - T0^4) can be shown, by expanding the fourth powers, to be approximately proportional to the temperature difference (T - T0). Hence Newton's law of cooling states that the RATE OF COOLING of a body is directly proportional to the excess of its temperature over that of the surroundings, provided that excess is small:

   dQ/dt = - k (T - T0)

Consequently a hot body cools quickly at first (large temperature excess) and more and more slowly as it approaches room temperature - a graph of temperature against time is a curve that flattens out towards T0. Newton's law of cooling is the basis of a standard laboratory method for comparing the specific heats of liquids.

Worked example 3. A body cools from 70 C to 60 C in 5 minutes when the room is at 30 C. Estimate the time to cool from 60 C to 50 C.
Solution. Using the average-excess form of Newton's law: for the first stage the average temperature is 65 C, excess = 35 C, and it lost 10 C in 5 min, so rate constant relation gives 10/5 = k(35). For the second stage the average temperature is 55 C, excess = 25 C: 10/t = k(25). Dividing, (10/t)/(10/5) = 25/35, so 5/t = 25/35, t = 5 x 35/25 = 7 minutes. The body cools more slowly as it nears the room temperature.

10.5 WIEN'S DISPLACEMENT LAW AND KIRCHHOFF'S LAW

Black-body spectrum. A black body does not emit at a single wavelength but over a continuous range. If the emitted power per unit wavelength is plotted against wavelength, the curve rises to a peak at some wavelength lambda_m and then falls off. As the temperature is raised, the whole curve rises and its peak shifts towards SHORTER wavelengths.

Wien's displacement law. The wavelength lambda_m at which the emission is maximum is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature:

   lambda_m T = b

where b is WIEN'S CONSTANT, b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K (2.898 x 10^-3 m K). This is why a body glows first dull red, then orange, yellow and finally bluish-white as it is made hotter - the peak of its radiation moves from the long-wavelength (red) end towards shorter wavelengths. Wien's law lets astronomers estimate the surface temperature of a star from the colour (peak wavelength) of its light.

Worked example 4. The Sun's radiation peaks at about lambda_m = 500 nm = 5.0 x 10^-7 m. Estimate the Sun's surface temperature.
Solution. T = b / lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3 / (5.0 x 10^-7) = 5800 K (approximately). This agrees well with the accepted photospheric temperature of about 5800 K.

Kirchhoff's law. At a given temperature and wavelength, the ratio of the emissive power to the absorptance is the SAME for all bodies and equals the emissive power of a black body. In simple words: GOOD ABSORBERS ARE GOOD EMITTERS. A surface that absorbs strongly at a certain wavelength also emits strongly at that same wavelength when heated. This explains why a dull black kettle cools faster than a polished one, and why the dark lines (Fraunhofer lines) in the Sun's spectrum correspond exactly to wavelengths that the cooler outer gases can absorb.

10.6 THE GREENHOUSE EFFECT

The Sun, being very hot (about 5800 K), radiates mostly at short wavelengths (visible and near-infrared). This short-wave radiation passes easily through the glass of a greenhouse (or through the atmosphere). It is absorbed by the soil, plants and objects inside, which warm up. Being much cooler (near 300 K), these bodies re-radiate energy at much LONGER (far-infrared) wavelengths - and glass (and certain atmospheric gases) is opaque to this long-wave radiation. The re-radiated heat is therefore trapped inside, and the temperature rises. This is the GREENHOUSE EFFECT.

In the atmosphere the role of the glass is played by GREENHOUSE GASES - carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane and others. They let sunlight in but absorb the outgoing infrared radiation from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet about 33 C warmer than it would otherwise be - warm enough for life. However, the burning of fossil fuels has increased the concentration of these gases, enhancing the effect and causing GLOBAL WARMING and climate change.

10.7 SOLAR ENERGY AND SOLAR DEVICES

The Sun is the ultimate source of almost all energy on Earth. The SOLAR CONSTANT is the amount of solar energy received per unit time on a unit area held perpendicular to the Sun's rays, just outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the mean Earth-Sun distance. Its value is about 1.36 kW/m^2 (roughly 1.4 kW/m^2, or about 1360 W/m^2). After absorption and scattering in the atmosphere, roughly 1 kW/m^2 reaches the ground on a clear day. Solar energy is clean, renewable and free, but it is dilute (spread thinly), intermittent (available only by day and in good weather), and needs large collecting areas.

Solar cooker. A box-type solar cooker is an insulated box with a blackened interior and a glass cover, often with a plane mirror reflector to direct extra sunlight in. Sunlight enters through the glass, is absorbed by the black surface and the cooking vessels (which are painted black to absorb well), and the glass then traps the re-radiated long-wave heat by the greenhouse effect. Temperatures of 100-140 C can be reached - enough to cook rice, pulses and vegetables slowly. It saves fuel and produces no smoke, but cannot fry or bake and does not work at night or under cloud.

Solar cell (photovoltaic cell). A solar cell converts sunlight DIRECTLY into electricity using a semiconductor (usually silicon) p-n junction. When light falls on the junction, photons free electron-hole pairs and the junction's built-in field drives them to the terminals, producing a small voltage (about 0.5 V per cell). Cells are connected in series and parallel to form panels and arrays. Solar cells power calculators, street lights, satellites, water pumps and homes; they have no moving parts and need little maintenance, though their efficiency is modest and they need sunlight.

Solar water heater. A solar water heater uses a flat-plate collector: a blackened copper (or aluminium) absorber plate with water pipes bonded to it, enclosed in an insulated box with a glass top. Sunlight heats the black plate, which heats the water in the pipes. The warm, less dense water rises by natural convection (a thermosiphon) into an insulated storage tank, while cold water flows down to be heated - so the system circulates on its own without a pump. Such heaters routinely supply hot water at 60-80 C for homes and hostels.

SUMMARY

- Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter to a colder body by three mechanisms: conduction, convection and radiation.
- Conduction transfers heat through matter without bulk motion; heat current H = K A (T1 - T2)/L; thermal resistance R = L/(KA); resistances add in series and combine reciprocally in parallel.
- Convection transfers heat by bulk movement of a fluid; it is natural (density driven) or forced (fan/pump driven); it cannot occur in solids or a vacuum.
- Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium. A perfect black body absorbs and emits ideally; emissivity e compares a real surface with a black body.
- Stefan-Boltzmann law: E = sigma T^4 (net E = e sigma (T^4 - T0^4)); sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4.
- Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling is proportional to the (small) temperature excess over the surroundings.
- Wien's displacement law: lambda_m T = b, b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K; hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.
- Kirchhoff's law: good absorbers are good emitters.
- The greenhouse effect traps long-wave re-radiated heat; greenhouse gases cause global warming.
- The solar constant is about 1.36 kW/m^2. Solar cookers (greenhouse box), solar cells (photovoltaic) and solar water heaters (flat-plate thermosiphon) harness solar energy.

chapter_summary.title: Heat Transfer and Solar Energy - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) summary covers the three modes of heat transfer - conduction, convection and radiation - the laws of thermal radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann, Newton's cooling, Wien and Kirchhoff), the greenhouse effect, and the harnessing of solar energy in cookers, cells and water heaters.

sections.heading: Conduction
bullets: Conduction transfers heat through a material from molecule to molecule (and by free electrons in metals) without any bulk movement of the material.
The steady heat current is H = K A (T1 - T2)/L, where K is the thermal conductivity (W/m/K) and (T1 - T2)/L is the temperature gradient.
Thermal resistance R = L/(KA) is measured in K/W; a thick, small-area, low-K slab has a high resistance and passes little heat.
For slabs in series the resistances add (R = R1 + R2); for slabs in parallel they combine reciprocally (1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2).

sections.heading: Convection
bullets: Convection transfers heat by the actual bulk movement of a heated fluid; warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, setting up a convection current.
Natural (free) convection is driven only by density differences (boiling water, sea and land breezes); forced convection uses a fan or pump and is faster.
Convection cannot occur in solids (particles not free to move) nor in a vacuum (no medium).

sections.heading: Radiation and the black body
bullets: Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; solar energy reaches Earth this way.
For incident radiation, absorptance + reflectance + transmittance = 1; a perfect black body absorbs all radiation (a = 1) and is also the best emitter.
Emissive power is the energy radiated per unit area per unit time; emissivity e (0 to 1) compares a real surface with a black body; good absorbers are good emitters.

sections.heading: Laws of thermal radiation
bullets: Stefan-Boltzmann law: a black body radiates E = sigma T^4 per unit area, with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4; net loss = e sigma (T^4 - T0^4).
Newton's law of cooling: for a small temperature excess, the rate of cooling is proportional to (T - T0), so a hot body cools fast at first, then slower.
Wien's displacement law: lambda_m T = b (b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K); hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths, so glow shifts red to white.
Kirchhoff's law: at a given temperature and wavelength, good absorbers are good emitters.

sections.heading: Greenhouse effect and solar devices
bullets: The greenhouse effect: short-wave sunlight enters glass (or atmosphere), is absorbed and re-radiated as long-wave infrared, which is trapped, raising the temperature.
Greenhouse gases (CO2, water vapour, methane) trap outgoing infrared; their increase causes global warming.
The solar constant is about 1.36 kW/m^2; solar energy is clean and renewable but dilute and intermittent.
Solar cooker (blackened insulated box with glass), solar cell (photovoltaic p-n junction giving electricity) and solar water heater (flat-plate thermosiphon) harness solar energy.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Heat Transfer and Solar Energy (NIOS)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Take sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4 and Wien's constant b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K where required. Show your working for numerical problems.

questions.question: Name the three modes of heat transfer and state, for each, whether it needs a material medium.
questions.answer: The three modes are: (1) CONDUCTION - needs a material medium (heat passes molecule to molecule; no bulk motion). (2) CONVECTION - needs a material medium that can flow (a liquid or gas moves in bulk). (3) RADIATION - needs NO medium; heat travels as electromagnetic waves, even through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Conduction and convection need matter; radiation does not.

questions.question: A glass window of area 2.0 m^2 and thickness 5.0 mm has its inner face at 25 C and outer face at 10 C. Taking K(glass) = 0.80 W/m/K, calculate the rate of heat flow through it.
questions.explanation: Direct application of H = K A (T1-T2)/L with L in metres.

questions.question: Distinguish between natural convection and forced convection, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: NATURAL (free) convection: the fluid circulates only because of density differences produced by heating - warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, with no external help. Example: water boiling in a pan, or a sea breeze. FORCED convection: an external agent (fan, pump, blower) drives the fluid past the hot surface, transferring heat much faster. Example: a car radiator with its fan, or a hair dryer.
questions.explanation: Natural = density-driven; forced = machine-driven.

questions.question: What is a perfect black body? State two of its properties.
questions.answer: A PERFECT BLACK BODY is one that absorbs all the radiation of every wavelength falling on it (absorptance = 1), reflecting and transmitting none. Properties: (1) It is the best possible ABSORBER of radiation. (2) At any given temperature it is also the best possible EMITTER of radiation. A small hole in a hollow cavity acts almost as a black body.
questions.explanation: Absorbs everything; also the ideal emitter.

questions.question: A black body of surface area 5.0 x 10^-3 m^2 is maintained at 800 K. Using the Stefan-Boltzmann law, find the power it radiates. (sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4.)
questions.explanation: E = sigma T^4, then multiply by area.

questions.question: The radiation from a certain star peaks at a wavelength of 1.0 x 10^-7 m. Estimate the surface temperature of the star using Wien's displacement law (b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K).
questions.answer: By Wien's law lambda_m T = b, so T = b/lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3 / (1.0 x 10^-7) = 2.9 x 10^4 = 29000 K. The star's surface temperature is about 29000 K - a very hot, bluish-white star.
questions.explanation: T = b/lambda_m.

questions.question: State Newton's law of cooling. A body cools from 80 C to 70 C in 5 minutes in surroundings at 30 C. Estimate how long it will take to cool from 70 C to 60 C. Explain why the second stage takes longer.
questions.answer:
Newton's law of cooling: the rate of cooling of a body is directly proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings, provided the excess is small: dQ/dt = -k(T - T0).
Stage 1: temperature falls 80 to 70 C in 5 min; average temperature 75 C, excess over 30 C = 45. So 10/5 = k(45), giving 2 = 45k.
Stage 2: 70 to 60 C; average 65 C, excess = 35. So 10/t = k(35).
Dividing: (10/t)/(10/5) = 35/45, i.e. 5/t = 35/45, so t = 5 x 45/35 = 6.4 minutes (about 6 min 26 s).
The second stage takes longer because the temperature excess over the surroundings is smaller, so by Newton's law the rate of cooling is smaller - the body cools more and more slowly as it nears room temperature.
questions.explanation: State the law, apply average-excess method, and reason about the slowing rate.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect and name two greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: The GREENHOUSE EFFECT: the Sun (very hot) sends mostly short-wave radiation, which passes easily through glass or the atmosphere and is absorbed by objects/soil inside. These cooler bodies re-radiate energy as long-wave (far-infrared) radiation, to which glass and certain gases are opaque. The long-wave heat is therefore trapped, raising the temperature. Two greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapour (also methane).
questions.explanation: Short-wave in, long-wave trapped; CO2 and water vapour.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a box-type solar cooker. State one advantage and one limitation.
questions.answer:
CONSTRUCTION: a box-type solar cooker is a well-insulated box with a blackened (matt black) interior, a double glass cover (lid) on top, and often a plane mirror reflector hinged to the lid to direct extra sunlight in. Cooking vessels are painted black.
WORKING: sunlight passes through the glass lid and is absorbed by the black interior and black vessels, which heat up. The glass then traps the long-wave heat re-radiated by the hot interior (the greenhouse effect), so the temperature builds up to 100-140 C - enough to cook rice, pulses and vegetables slowly. The reflector increases the sunlight collected.
ADVANTAGE: it uses free, clean, renewable solar energy and produces no smoke or fuel cost. LIMITATION: it works only in bright sunshine (not at night or in cloud), cooks slowly, and cannot fry or bake.
questions.explanation: Insulated blackened glass-topped box using the greenhouse effect; clean but slow and weather-dependent.

questions.question: Two slabs of the same area, with thermal resistances R1 = 2 K/W and R2 = 3 K/W, are joined one behind the other (in series) between faces at 100 C and 0 C. Find the heat current through them.
questions.answer: In series the resistances add: R = R1 + R2 = 2 + 3 = 5 K/W. The temperature difference is 100 - 0 = 100 K (equal to 100 C difference). Heat current H = (T1 - T2)/R = 100/5 = 20 W. The same 20 W flows through both slabs.
questions.explanation: Series resistances add; H = deltaT / R_total.

through matter without bulk movement of the material
questions.answer: through matter without bulk movement of the material
questions.explanation: Molecule to molecule; the material itself does not move.

no heat is stored, so the same amount that enters must leave

questions.question: Define thermal conductivity and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY (K) of a material is the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient in the steady state; from H = K A (T1 - T2)/L it is the heat current per unit area per unit temperature gradient. Its SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin (W/m/K). Metals have high K; insulators have low K.

questions.question: Why does a metal object feel colder to the touch than a wooden object at the same temperature?
questions.answer: Both are at the same temperature, but metal has a much higher thermal conductivity than wood. When you touch the metal, it conducts heat away from your warm skin rapidly, so your skin cools quickly and the metal feels cold. Wood conducts heat away slowly, so it does not draw heat from the skin as fast and feels comparatively warm.

questions.question: A copper rod of length 0.20 m and cross-sectional area 4.0 x 10^-4 m^2 has its ends at 100 C and 0 C. Taking K(copper) = 400 W/m/K, find the heat current.
Define thermal resistance and state how thermal resistances combine in series.
questions.answer: THERMAL RESISTANCE R of a slab is its opposition to heat flow, R = L/(KA), measured in K/W; the heat current is H = (T1 - T2)/R. When slabs are connected in SERIES (one behind the other, same heat current through each), their resistances ADD: R = R1 + R2 + ... , just like resistors in series in an electric circuit.

questions.question: Two slabs of equal area, thermal resistances 4 K/W and 4 K/W, are joined in series between surfaces at 80 C and 0 C. Find (a) the total resistance and (b) the heat current.
questions.answer: (a) In series, resistances add: R = 4 + 4 = 8 K/W. (b) The temperature difference is 80 - 0 = 80 K. Heat current H = (T1 - T2)/R = 80/8 = 10 W. The same 10 W flows through both slabs.

questions.question: Explain how a convection current is set up when water is heated in a pan from below.
questions.answer: When the water at the bottom is heated, it expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler, denser water from the top sinks to take its place. This continuous circulation of rising warm water and sinking cool water is a CONVECTION CURRENT, and it distributes heat throughout the pan until all the water is hot.

questions.question: Give two everyday examples of natural convection.
questions.answer: (1) SEA AND LAND BREEZES: during the day the land heats faster than the sea, so warm air over the land rises and cooler air from the sea flows in (sea breeze); at night the flow reverses (land breeze). (2) BOILING WATER in a pan, where hot water rises and cool water sinks. (Other examples: warm air rising above a heater, ventilation of rooms.)

questions.question: Why are ventilators and windows usually placed near the top of a room, while a room heater is placed near the floor?
questions.answer: This uses natural convection. Warm air is less dense and rises, while cool air is denser and sinks. A heater placed near the FLOOR heats the lower air, which rises and warms the whole room by convection, drawing cool air down to be heated - an efficient circulation. Ventilators near the TOP let the warm, stale, used air (which has risen) escape, so fresh cooler air enters from lower openings. Placing them the other way round would trap warm air at the ceiling and fail to circulate it.

questions.question: State two ways in which radiation differs from conduction and convection.
questions.answer: (1) Radiation does NOT need any material medium - it travels through a vacuum (e.g. the Sun's heat reaching Earth); conduction and convection both need matter. (2) Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves at the speed of light, whereas conduction passes energy molecule to molecule and convection carries it by the slow bulk movement of a fluid.

questions.question: What is meant by the emissivity of a surface? What are its values for a perfect black body and a perfect reflector?
questions.answer: EMISSIVITY (e) is the ratio of the emissive power of a real surface to that of a perfect black body at the same temperature; it measures how good a radiator the surface is. For a perfect black body e = 1 (best emitter); for a perfect reflector (a perfectly shiny surface) e is close to 0 (radiates almost nothing). Real surfaces lie between these limits.

questions.question: Why are cooking vessels often blackened at the bottom but tea is kept hot in shiny polished flasks?
questions.answer: A blackened bottom is a good ABSORBER (and emitter) of radiation, so it absorbs heat from the flame quickly and heats the food faster. A shiny polished flask surface is a poor emitter and a good reflector, so it radiates very little heat and reflects radiation back - this keeps the tea hot for longer by minimising radiative heat loss. Both follow from the rule that good absorbers/emitters are dull black while poor emitters are shiny.

questions.question: State the Stefan-Boltzmann law and give the value of the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.
questions.answer: The STEFAN-BOLTZMANN LAW states that the total energy radiated per unit area per unit time by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: E = sigma T^4. The Stefan-Boltzmann constant is sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4. For a real body of emissivity e, E = e sigma T^4.

State Newton's law of cooling and explain why a hot body cools more slowly as it approaches room temperature.
questions.answer: Newton's law of cooling: the rate of cooling of a body is directly proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings, provided that excess is small: dQ/dt = -k(T - T0). As the body cools, its temperature excess (T - T0) becomes smaller, so the rate of cooling becomes smaller too. Therefore the body cools quickly at first and more and more slowly as it nears room temperature - its temperature-time graph flattens towards T0.

questions.question: The temperature of a black body is raised from 300 K to 900 K. By what factor does its rate of radiation per unit area increase?
questions.answer: By the Stefan-Boltzmann law, E is proportional to T^4. The factor is (T2/T1)^4 = (900/300)^4 = 3^4 = 81. So the rate of radiation per unit area increases 81 times.

questions.question: State Wien's displacement law and give the value of Wien's constant.
questions.answer: WIEN'S DISPLACEMENT LAW: the wavelength lambda_m at which a black body emits maximum energy is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature, i.e. lambda_m T = b, where b is Wien's constant = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K (2.898 x 10^-3 m K). As T rises, lambda_m decreases, so the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths.

questions.question: The Sun's radiation is most intense at a wavelength of about 4.83 x 10^-7 m. Estimate the Sun's surface temperature. (b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K.)
questions.answer: By Wien's law, T = b/lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3 / (4.83 x 10^-7) = 6004 K, about 6000 K. This agrees with the Sun's surface (photosphere) temperature of roughly 5800-6000 K.

questions.question: State Kirchhoff's law of radiation and give one everyday consequence of it.
questions.answer: KIRCHHOFF'S LAW: at a given temperature and wavelength, the ratio of the emissive power to the absorptance is the same for all bodies and equals the emissive power of a black body - in short, GOOD ABSORBERS ARE GOOD EMITTERS. Everyday consequence: a dull black surface, being a good absorber, also radiates (and hence cools) faster than a shiny polished surface, which is why radiators and cooking pans are often blackened.

questions.question: What is the solar constant? State its approximate value.
questions.answer: The SOLAR CONSTANT is the amount of solar energy received per unit time on a unit area held perpendicular to the Sun's rays, just outside the Earth's atmosphere, at the mean Earth-Sun distance. Its approximate value is 1.36 kW/m^2 (about 1360 W/m^2). After atmospheric losses, roughly 1 kW/m^2 reaches the ground on a clear day.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect and state how it is linked to global warming.
questions.answer: The Sun (about 5800 K) radiates mostly short-wave (visible) light, which passes through glass or the atmosphere and is absorbed by surfaces, warming them. These cooler surfaces re-radiate energy as long-wave infrared, to which glass and greenhouse gases are opaque, so this heat is trapped and the temperature rises - the GREENHOUSE EFFECT. In the atmosphere, greenhouse gases (CO2, water vapour, methane) do this naturally, keeping Earth warm enough for life. But burning fossil fuels raises their concentration, trapping more heat and causing GLOBAL WARMING and climate change.

questions.question: State two advantages and one limitation of a solar cooker.
questions.answer: ADVANTAGES: (1) it uses free, clean, renewable solar energy, so there is no fuel cost; (2) it produces no smoke or pollution and needs no electricity or gas. LIMITATION: it works only in bright sunshine (not at night or in cloudy weather), cooks slowly, and cannot fry or bake food.

questions.question: Describe how a flat-plate solar water heater works.
questions.answer: A flat-plate solar water heater has a blackened copper absorber plate with water pipes bonded to it, enclosed in an insulated box with a glass top. Sunlight passes through the glass and heats the black plate (the glass also traps re-radiated heat by the greenhouse effect). The plate heats the water in the pipes; the warm, less dense water rises by natural convection (a thermosiphon) into an insulated storage tank, while cold water flows down to be heated. Thus the water circulates by itself without a pump and hot water at 60-80 C collects in the tank.

questions.question: Derive/state the expression for the heat current through a conducting slab and define thermal resistance. Then find the heat current through a slab of area 0.50 m^2, thickness 0.10 m and conductivity 0.20 W/m/K whose faces are at 90 C and 10 C.
questions.answer:
For a slab of area A and thickness L with faces at steady temperatures T1 and T2 (T1 > T2), experiment shows the heat conducted in time t is Q = K A (T1 - T2) t / L, so the HEAT CURRENT is H = Q/t = K A (T1 - T2)/L, where K is the thermal conductivity and (T1 - T2)/L is the temperature gradient. Writing this as H = (T1 - T2)/R defines the THERMAL RESISTANCE R = L/(KA), measured in K/W - the electrical analogue where H plays the role of current and (T1 - T2) the role of voltage.
Numerical: H = K A (T1 - T2)/L = 0.20 x 0.50 x (90 - 10)/0.10 = 0.20 x 0.50 x 80 / 0.10 = 8.0 / 0.10 = 80 W. So the heat current is 80 W. (Check with resistance: R = L/(KA) = 0.10/(0.20 x 0.50) = 1.0 K/W; H = 80/1.0 = 80 W.)

questions.question: Compare the three modes of heat transfer - conduction, convection and radiation - under the headings: (i) mechanism, (ii) need for a medium, (iii) an everyday example.
questions.answer:
CONDUCTION: (i) mechanism - heat passes from molecule to molecule (and by free electrons in metals) with NO bulk movement of the material; (ii) needs a material medium (usually a solid); (iii) example - the far end of a metal spoon heating up when one end is in hot tea.
CONVECTION: (i) mechanism - a heated fluid moves in BULK, warm fluid rising and cool fluid sinking, setting up convection currents; (ii) needs a fluid medium (liquid or gas); (iii) example - water boiling in a pan, or sea breezes.
RADIATION: (i) mechanism - energy travels as ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES; (ii) needs NO medium, travels through a vacuum; (iii) example - the Sun's heat reaching the Earth, or warmth felt near a fire. In summary, conduction and convection require matter, while radiation does not.

questions.question: Explain what happens when thermal radiation falls on a body, defining absorptance, reflectance and transmittance. Hence explain what a perfect black body is and why it is also a perfect emitter.
questions.answer:
When radiation of energy falls on a body, it is split three ways: part is ABSORBED, part is REFLECTED, and part is TRANSMITTED (passes through). The fractions are the ABSORPTANCE a, the REFLECTANCE r and the TRANSMITTANCE, and by energy conservation a + r + transmittance = 1. A surface that absorbs strongly reflects and transmits little, and vice versa.
A PERFECT BLACK BODY is one for which a = 1 - it absorbs ALL the radiation of every wavelength falling on it, reflecting and transmitting nothing (r = 0, transmittance = 0). A small hole in a hollow cavity is a good practical black body, because radiation entering the hole is reflected repeatedly inside and almost none comes out.
By Kirchhoff's law, at a given temperature good absorbers are good emitters. Since a black body is the best possible absorber, it must also be the best possible EMITTER at any temperature - so a black body both absorbs and radiates ideally.

questions.question: State the Stefan-Boltzmann law. A spherical black body of radius 0.050 m is maintained at 1000 K in surroundings at 300 K. Calculate the net rate at which it loses energy by radiation. (sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4; surface area of a sphere = 4 pi r^2.)
questions.answer:
STEFAN-BOLTZMANN LAW: a black body radiates energy per unit area per unit time E = sigma T^4; the NET loss per unit area to surroundings at T0 is sigma (T^4 - T0^4).
Surface area A = 4 pi r^2 = 4 x 3.14 x (0.050)^2 = 4 x 3.14 x 0.0025 = 0.0314 m^2.
T^4 = (1000)^4 = 1.0 x 10^12; T0^4 = (300)^4 = 8.1 x 10^9. Difference = 1.0 x 10^12 - 0.081 x 10^12 = 0.919 x 10^12 = 9.19 x 10^11.
Net loss per unit area = sigma (T^4 - T0^4) = 5.67 x 10^-8 x 9.19 x 10^11 = 5.21 x 10^4 W/m^2.
Net power lost = 5.21 x 10^4 x 0.0314 = 1636 W, about 1.6 kW. (Because T is much larger than T0, most of the loss comes from the T^4 term.)

questions.question: State Wien's displacement law and explain, using it, why a heated iron rod changes colour from dull red to bluish-white as it gets hotter. Estimate the temperature at which lambda_m = 700 nm (red). (b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K.)
questions.answer:
WIEN'S DISPLACEMENT LAW: the wavelength of maximum emission of a black body obeys lambda_m T = b (b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K), so lambda_m is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature.
As an iron rod is heated, its temperature rises, so lambda_m decreases and the PEAK of its radiation moves from the long-wavelength (red) end toward shorter wavelengths. At first the rod glows dull RED (long wavelengths only); as it gets hotter the peak shifts to orange, then yellow, and finally the emission spreads across all visible wavelengths so the rod looks bluish-WHITE. Thus colour is a rough thermometer of temperature.
At lambda_m = 700 nm = 7.0 x 10^-7 m: T = b/lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3 / (7.0 x 10^-7) = 4143 K, about 4100 K.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect? Explain its mechanism, its natural benefit, and how human activity is turning it into a problem.
questions.answer:
The GREENHOUSE EFFECT is the trapping of heat by glass or by the atmosphere. MECHANISM: the Sun, being very hot (~5800 K), radiates mostly short-wave (visible/near-infrared) radiation, which passes easily through glass or the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground, plants and objects, warming them. Being much cooler (~300 K), these surfaces re-radiate energy at long (far-infrared) wavelengths, to which glass and certain gases are opaque; this long-wave radiation is trapped, raising the temperature.
NATURAL BENEFIT: greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane) in the atmosphere trap enough outgoing infrared to keep the Earth about 33 C warmer than it would otherwise be - warm enough to support life. Without them the Earth would be frozen.
HUMAN PROBLEM: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) and deforestation have raised the concentration of CO2 and other greenhouse gases. This traps MORE outgoing infrared, enhancing the effect and causing GLOBAL WARMING, melting ice, rising sea levels and climate change.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of (a) a solar cell and (b) a box-type solar cooker. State one use of each.
questions.answer:
(a) SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic cell): CONSTRUCTION - a thin wafer of a semiconductor, usually silicon, forming a p-n junction with metal contacts on top and bottom. WORKING - when sunlight falls on the junction, photons free electron-hole pairs; the built-in electric field of the junction drives electrons one way and holes the other, producing a small voltage (about 0.5 V per cell). Cells are joined in series/parallel to form panels giving useful power. USE: powering calculators, street lights, satellites, water pumps and homes.
(b) BOX-TYPE SOLAR COOKER: CONSTRUCTION - a well-insulated box with a matt-black interior, a double glass lid, and often a plane mirror reflector; cooking vessels are painted black. WORKING - sunlight enters through the glass, is absorbed by the black interior and vessels which heat up, and the glass traps the re-radiated long-wave heat (greenhouse effect), raising the temperature to 100-140 C. The reflector adds extra sunlight. USE: cooking rice, pulses and vegetables using free, smoke-free solar energy.

questions.question: Explain, with reasons, the formation of land and sea breezes as examples of natural convection.
questions.answer:
Land and sea breezes arise because land and water heat and cool at different rates, setting up natural convection currents in the air.
SEA BREEZE (daytime): during the day the land heats up faster than the sea (land has a lower specific heat). The air over the warm land becomes hot, expands, becomes less dense and RISES. Cooler, denser air from over the sea flows in towards the land to take its place - this cool wind from sea to land is the SEA BREEZE.
LAND BREEZE (night-time): at night the land cools faster than the sea, so now the air over the (relatively warmer) sea is warmer, rises, and cooler air from the land flows out towards the sea - the LAND BREEZE, blowing from land to sea.
In both cases warm air rising and cooler air moving in to replace it is a convection current driven purely by density differences (natural convection), with no fan or pump involved.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Heat conduction through a slab in the steady state follows H = K A (T1 - T2)/L, where K is the thermal conductivity, A the area, L the thickness and (T1 - T2) the temperature difference between the faces.

(i) What does the symbol K represent, and what is its SI unit?
(ii) What is the name of the quantity (T1 - T2)/L?
(iii) A slab has A = 2.0 m^2, L = 0.10 m, K = 0.5 W/m/K, T1 = 40 C, T2 = 20 C. Find the heat current.
(iv) State how H changes if the thickness L is doubled.
questions.answer:
(i) K is the THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY of the material - the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient. Its SI unit is W/m/K.
(ii) (T1 - T2)/L is the TEMPERATURE GRADIENT (fall of temperature per unit length).
(iii) H = K A (T1 - T2)/L = 0.5 x 2.0 x (40 - 20)/0.10 = 0.5 x 2.0 x 20 / 0.10 = 20/0.10 = 200 W.
(iv) H is inversely proportional to L, so doubling L HALVES the heat current (to 100 W).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The thermal resistance of a slab is R = L/(KA). Resistances add in series (R = R1 + R2) and combine reciprocally in parallel (1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2). The heat current is H = (T1 - T2)/R.

(i) What is the SI unit of thermal resistance?
(ii) Two slabs of resistance 2 K/W and 3 K/W are joined in series across 100 C and 0 C. Find the total resistance and the heat current.
(iii) If instead the same two slabs are placed in parallel across the same 100 C difference, find the combined resistance.
(iv) In which arrangement is the heat current greater?
questions.answer:
(i) The SI unit of thermal resistance is K/W (kelvin per watt).
(ii) Series: R = 2 + 3 = 5 K/W. Temperature difference = 100 K. H = 100/5 = 20 W.
(iii) Parallel: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, so R = 6/5 = 1.2 K/W.
(iv) The PARALLEL arrangement has the lower resistance (1.2 K/W vs 5 K/W), so it carries the greater heat current (H = 100/1.2 = 83.3 W, much more than 20 W).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Convection transfers heat by the bulk movement of a fluid. In natural convection the flow is driven by density differences; in forced convection an external fan or pump drives the fluid. Convection cannot occur in solids or in a vacuum.

(i) Why can convection not occur in a solid?
(ii) Give one example each of natural and forced convection.
(iii) Why does warm air rise in natural convection?
(iv) Why can convection not occur in a vacuum?
questions.answer:
(i) In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions and cannot move in bulk, so no convection current can form.
(ii) Natural convection - boiling water in a pan (or a sea breeze). Forced convection - a room cooled by a ceiling fan (or a car radiator with its fan).
(iii) When air is heated it expands and becomes less dense than the surrounding cooler air; being lighter, it rises, while cooler denser air sinks to replace it.
(iv) A vacuum contains no matter, and convection needs a fluid (matter that can move) to carry the heat - so convection is impossible in a vacuum.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When radiation falls on a body, part is absorbed, part reflected and part transmitted, with a + r + transmittance = 1. A perfect black body absorbs everything (a = 1). Emissivity e compares a real surface's emission with that of a black body.

(i) Write the energy-balance relation for incident radiation.
(ii) What is the absorptance of a perfect black body?
(iii) What is the emissivity of (a) a black body and (b) a perfect reflector?
(iv) Why does radiation, unlike conduction and convection, not need a medium?
questions.answer:
(i) absorptance a + reflectance r + transmittance = 1 (the fractions of incident energy).
(ii) For a perfect black body, absorptance a = 1 (it absorbs all incident radiation).
(iii) (a) A black body has emissivity e = 1 (the best emitter). (b) A perfect reflector has emissivity e close to 0 (it radiates almost nothing).
(iv) Radiation is carried by electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space; conduction needs matter to pass energy molecule to molecule and convection needs a fluid to move, so both require a material medium while radiation does not.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that a black body radiates E = sigma T^4 per unit area per unit time, with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2/K^4. The net loss to surroundings at T0 is e sigma (T^4 - T0^4).

(i) Why must T be in kelvin?
(ii) A black body at 300 K is heated to 600 K. By what factor does its radiated power increase?
(iii) A black body of area 0.020 m^2 is at 500 K. Find the power it radiates.
(iv) Write the expression for the net rate of heat loss per unit area.
questions.answer:
(i) Because the law involves T^4, an absolute (kelvin) scale is essential; using Celsius would give wrong ratios and even negative temperatures.
(ii) Power scales as T^4, so the factor is (600/300)^4 = 2^4 = 16 times.
(iii) E = sigma T^4 = 5.67 x 10^-8 x (500)^4 = 5.67 x 10^-8 x 6.25 x 10^10 = 3543.75 W/m^2. Power = E x A = 3543.75 x 0.020 = 70.9 W (about 71 W).
(iv) Net rate of heat loss per unit area = e sigma (T^4 - T0^4).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Newton's law of cooling states that, for a small temperature excess, the rate of cooling of a body is proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings: dQ/dt = -k(T - T0).

(i) Under what condition is Newton's law of cooling valid?
(ii) A body cools from 60 C to 50 C in 4 minutes when the room is at 20 C. Using average temperatures, estimate the time to cool from 50 C to 40 C.
(iii) Why does the second stage take longer?
(iv) Sketch in words the shape of the temperature-time cooling curve.
questions.answer:
(i) It is valid when the temperature EXCESS of the body over its surroundings is SMALL.
(ii) Stage 1: average temp 55 C, excess 35; lost 10 C in 4 min, so 10/4 = k(35). Stage 2: average temp 45 C, excess 25; 10/t = k(25). Dividing: (10/t)/(10/4) = 25/35, so 4/t = 25/35, t = 4 x 35/25 = 5.6 minutes.
(iii) The temperature excess over the surroundings is smaller in the second stage, so by Newton's law the rate of cooling is smaller and it takes longer to lose the same 10 C.
(iv) The curve starts steep (fast cooling at high excess) and gradually flattens, approaching the room temperature T0 asymptotically - an exponential-like decay curve.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Wien's displacement law states lambda_m T = b, with b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K, where lambda_m is the wavelength of maximum emission. Kirchhoff's law states that good absorbers are good emitters.

(i) How does lambda_m change as a body gets hotter?
(ii) A body's radiation peaks at 5.8 x 10^-7 m. Find its temperature.
(iii) A blue star and a red star - which is hotter, and why?
(iv) State Kirchhoff's law in one sentence.
questions.answer:
(i) As the body gets hotter, its absolute temperature rises and lambda_m = b/T DECREASES, so the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths.
(ii) T = b/lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3 / (5.8 x 10^-7) = 5000 K.
(iii) The BLUE star is hotter. Blue light has a shorter peak wavelength than red, and by Wien's law a shorter lambda_m corresponds to a higher temperature.
(iv) Kirchhoff's law: at a given temperature and wavelength, a good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Sun radiates mostly short-wave radiation. This passes through glass or the atmosphere, is absorbed by surfaces, and is re-radiated as long-wave infrared, which glass and greenhouse gases trap. The solar constant is about 1.36 kW/m^2.

(i) What is the solar constant?
(ii) Why is short-wave sunlight able to enter a greenhouse while the re-radiated heat is trapped?
(iii) Name two greenhouse gases.
(iv) How does the greenhouse effect connect to global warming?
questions.answer:
(i) The solar constant is the solar energy received per unit time per unit area held perpendicular to the Sun's rays just outside the atmosphere, about 1.36 kW/m^2.
(ii) Glass (and the atmosphere) is transparent to short-wave (visible) radiation but opaque to long-wave (far-infrared) radiation. So sunlight enters, is absorbed and re-radiated at long wavelengths, which cannot escape and is trapped.
(iii) Carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapour (also methane).
(iv) Human activity (burning fossil fuels) increases greenhouse-gas concentrations, which trap more outgoing infrared radiation, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing global warming and climate change.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Solar devices harness the Sun's energy. A solar cooker uses a blackened insulated box with a glass cover; a solar cell converts sunlight directly into electricity; a solar water heater uses a flat-plate collector with a thermosiphon.

(i) On what physical effect does a box solar cooker work?
(ii) What energy conversion takes place in a solar cell?
(iii) Why is the absorber plate of a water heater painted black?
(iv) How does hot water rise into the storage tank without a pump?
questions.answer:
(i) A box solar cooker works on the GREENHOUSE EFFECT: the glass lets short-wave sunlight in, the black interior absorbs it, and the glass traps the re-radiated long-wave heat, raising the temperature.
(ii) A solar cell converts LIGHT ENERGY (sunlight) directly into ELECTRICAL ENERGY (photovoltaic effect in a silicon p-n junction).
(iii) A black plate is a good absorber of radiation, so it absorbs the maximum solar energy and heats the water most effectively.
(iv) The water heated in the collector becomes less dense and rises by NATURAL CONVECTION (a thermosiphon) into the insulated tank, while cooler denser water flows down to be heated - so it circulates without any pump.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A family installs a solar water heater on their roof. On a clear day the flat-plate collector receives about 1 kW/m^2 of sunlight. The blackened plate has area 2.0 m^2 and absorbs 60% of the incident energy.

(i) What power (in watts) does the plate absorb?
(ii) If all this power went into heating water, how much energy is collected in 1 hour?
(iii) Why is the collector covered with a glass sheet?
(iv) State one advantage and one limitation of this solar water heater.
questions.answer:
(i) Incident power = 1000 W/m^2 x 2.0 m^2 = 2000 W. Absorbed = 60% of 2000 = 0.60 x 2000 = 1200 W.
(ii) Energy in 1 hour = power x time = 1200 W x 3600 s = 4.32 x 10^6 J (4.32 MJ).
(iii) The glass sheet lets sunlight in but traps the re-radiated long-wave heat (greenhouse effect) and reduces convective heat loss, so the plate and water stay hotter.
(iv) Advantage: it provides free, clean, renewable hot water with no fuel cost and little maintenance. Limitation: it works only in sunny weather (not at night or under thick cloud) and needs a fairly large roof area.
